title: A single-player, creature collector, 6v6 auto-battler game where you collect blueprints, build machines, and program their combat behavior.
author: rdr2_fan7
selftext:
I’ve been working on Feramek Protocols for a few months now. It’s a single-player creature collector and 6v6 auto-battler where you collect blueprints, build machines, and program their combat behavior.

Please wishlist on Steam: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/542162](https://store.steampowered.com/app/542162)

comments.author: Frosty-Breath-81
comments.body:
your steam link got chopped off.

could be cool, but you need to polish the ai generated animations (manually). lots of inconsistencies which makes it look sloppy. the pixel art resolution of different things is all over the place too. creatures vs backgrounds vs foreground objects all look different. hard to tell from the trailer but is it all even pixel art? i mean, actually run thru pixelsnapper or something.

For a creature collector, I think the art direction and execution are exceptionally important for the fantasy aspect. If your game plays well (I have no idea, but auto battlers are popular) then you should really focus on the art aspect. You'll get chewed up in Steam reviews if your game continues to look like this.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
Oh, I like this conceptually. I dropped you a wishlist. Some things: 

 \- The link doesn't go to your game. I had to manually look it up. You'll probably want to fix that.

 \- It looks like your current art has a 'mixels' problem, where the pixels aren't real pixels. You'll want to put all of the sprites through a sprite snapper, then also get rid of the partial transparencies that will be present afterward, then clean-up the outlines. It's a lot of work, but it will pay off on multiple levels, including giving you clean sprites to work with for animations.

 \- There is significant stylistic contrast between the Pokemons and the environment art. You could probably solve that with color reduction of the Pokemons, though it would be at a cost of visual fidelity. 

Really, the better option is probably to just abandon the paid environment asset pack, as lovely as it looks on its own, and also generate the environment art just of the sake of visual consistency. Very, very hard to go in an fix all of it up, but rewarding and worth it in the end, IMHO.

replies.author: rdr2_fan7
replies.body: Hi! Thanks. Do you have any recommendation for the environment art? Like what tools do you use?

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body:
My current process is to generate pieces for the enviroment usng ChatGPT's imagegen, scale them with a pixel snapper (my snapper of choice is [this tool](https://portalrabbit.com/) , because it gives a lot of control over the snapping... realistically, though, you could probably have Astra make you a tool really quickly to do snapping for you) and build the scene.  
  
To get everything at a consistent size I set-up a downscaler canvas in GIMP with a single reference object. All objects I want to downscale are pasted into that canvas, macro-scaled to be at an appropriate size relative to the reference object, then I go to my pixel snapper, go to Grid Artist, and make sure I pick the same longest edge setting for each object that I want to have at the same relative scale.

Example: 

I'm currently building a parallax scene in a jungle. I want trees in the foreground, a river behind the trees, a distant community on a bit of a hill beyond the river. 

I ask imagegen to build me the tree foreground objects: 

*Niji anime style environmental belt-scroller game art.*

*A parallax background element that can infinitely scroll horizontally.*

*A strip of jungle trees, large boulders, lichen, giants flowers and thorny brambles, on a transparent background. The flowers are vibrant orange, purple, black and red in color - they're nearly as large as the trees. Vines hang down from the tops of the trees. There is dense green vegetation and tall grass.*

I don't ask it to create pixel art because I find it creates more problems later - it'll try to add outlines that will be mixels, meaning I have to do more clean-up after I snap the art to a grid. Also sometimes the mixels are just at the wrong scale, which makes pixel snapping them a nightmare. 

Niji-style anime art tends to have strong silhouettes, which is the most important thing for pixel snapping, IMHO.   
  
If you're not doing parallax, you don't need to ask for the infinite scrolling; if you want to be less lazy than me and get even nicer art, don't ask for the whole foreground scene like I did - ask for the individual trees, rocks, bushes, etc, and you'll have to put it all together yourself.  
  
First step is the downscaler canvas - I take the asset imagegen gave me and plop it into an 1800 x 1080 canvas. I scale each asset so their relative sizes match each other. Then I copy and paste each invidual object, with the correct relative scale, into the pixel snapper and always choose the same longest edge option. Copy them from the pixel snapper into a new canvas; they're all properly downscaled and de-slopped, I clean them up, I can put together a background environment with them like building a lego set.  
  
 To help save time and tokens, don't ask ChatGPT to make one object at a time. Ask it to produce a grid of variations on an object. Example:   
  
*Niji anime-style game sprite art*

*Please draw 9 variations of this concept in a 3x3 grid with a transparent background, with each variation occupying 1 cell of the grid:*

*A crow, both with in flight and on the ground poses.*

...Replace the crow with trees, shrubs, background cranes, buildings, cars, whatever you want the environment to have in it. That way you can generate sheets full of varying assets at once; you'll get much fewer outright failed generations because it's unlikely to just fail a whole sheet, and you'll get a lot of variety in props to build an environment with without having to name every single object one by one. 

Oh, and make sure you kill partial transparency with your sprites once you have them snapped. I can't tell you how to do that without knowing what art program you use; in GIMP, you just go Layer -> Transparency -> Threshold Alpha... 

The default setting for the GIMP method works like a charm.
